narrative:
The decision to deny your application was based on a prediction that you have a 95.9% chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. In other words, the model believes that if you were admitted to law school, you would be extremely likely to fall short of the professional licensing hurdle that follows graduation. This high risk of failure was the central reason your application was not accepted.

Looking at what drove this prediction, three factors stood out as most influential, ranked in order of strength. The single strongest influence was your class standing in your third year of study. You were in the bottom decile of your school, while accepted applicants typically sat much higher, around the middle of the pack. This suggests that your academic performance did not improve over time, which is a critical signal for bar readiness.

The next most important factor was your LSAT score. Your score of 26 is well below the average of 37 among accepted students. The LSAT measures reasoning skills that are directly tied to bar exam success, so a low score strongly pushed the prediction toward failure.

Finally, your first-year class standing also played a significant role. Again, you were in the bottom decile, while accepted students were typically around sixth decile. Both your early and late academic performance pointed the same direction.

Taken together, these three signals indicate that your current academic record and test-taking abilities are not yet at the level needed to pass the bar exam. The good news is that these are not fixed traits. To improve your chances, you should consider retaking the LSAT after intensive preparation and seeking feedback on your study habits. If you reapply later with a stronger LSAT score and a track record of improved grades, the model would likely see a much lower risk of failure.
